perspective:
I, Mason Hurley, have access to the following information:

- I am an accountant at a small community center. Martha Moua is a colleague there, a personal care aide. Our relationship is professional and mainly work-related; we are not personally close.
- I reviewed the recent financial reports and noticed discrepancies: healthcare expenses seemed unusually high and did not match usual spending patterns. This made me suspect Martha might be mismanaging funds, and I felt suspicious and anxious.
- I spoke with Martha about the report. She said there was likely a reasonable explanation, asked which discrepancies I meant, then said she saw the issue—possibly a misentry—and would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing with Martha, I understood the discrepancies were due to a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. I felt relieved but embarrassed. I thanked Martha, said it seemed to be just a clerical error, apologized for my initial suspicion, and said I should have asked her first.
- Martha told me errors happen, she was glad we cleared it up, she understood I was being thorough, and suggested double-checking entries next time.
- I later believed Martha was competent. I thought the recurring clerical errors showed the financial management system was inadequate, not Martha’s management. I felt frustrated with the system but empathetic toward Martha.
- I discussed prevention with Martha. I said the issue was the current system, proposed drafting a new, more robust financial system, and asked for her input. Martha agreed and offered to help address the gaps.
- I drafted a proposal. I was hopeful it would benefit operations but uncertain whether management would approve it. I told Martha I had finished the draft and shared my uncertainty. She called it solid and encouraged presenting it confidently. I agreed to prepare a detailed presentation and asked her to help gather data; she agreed.
- I presented the proposal to management. I felt satisfied with my effort but physically and mentally exhausted, believing I had done everything I could. I did not yet know management’s decision.
- I told Martha the presentation went well and that it was now up to management. She praised my work and suggested I take time off. I thanked her, said I would take a few days off to recharge and reflect, and hoped for good news. She told me to enjoy the break and let her know if I needed anything.
